structured_extraction.program_description: Howard County's Department of Housing and Community Development administers federal and local grant programs to support community development activities in Howard County. Programs include the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG), HOME Investment Partnerships, and other funding to support housing, public services, and community infrastructure. Howard County receives federal CDBG funds from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and distributes them to non-profits serving Howard County residents. CDBG funds support a variety of housing and community development activities that primarily benefit low- and moderate-income residents. The department provides financial and technical assistance to nonprofit organizations, community groups, government agencies, and residents for housing, community development, and related initiatives.
structured_extraction.agency: Howard County Department of Housing and Community Development
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Federal CDBG and HOME Investment Partnerships funds administered by Howard County DHCD for community development activities. FFY2025 CDBG allocation: $1,336,389; HOME $504,077.24. Funds are distributed countywide to nonprofits, for-profit agencies, and public agencies serving Howard County residents, primarily benefiting low- and moderate-income residents. Assistance types include grants, loans, guarantees, rental assistance, homebuyer assistance, housing rehabilitation, and emergency shelter operations. CDBG use of funds: Public Facilities (33%), Housing Activities (42%), Public Services (15%). Rental affordability standards tied to 80% AMI or HUD Fair Market Rent. Specific award amounts, terms, and mechanics vary by program and are determined through the Annual Action Plan process each program year (July 1 – June 30).
structured_extraction.program_audience: Nonprofit organizations, for-profit developers, government agencies, community groups, and residents in Howard County — including those serving low- and moderate-income residents, seniors (62+), persons with disabilities, homeless individuals and families, domestic violence survivors, formerly homeless individuals, families with children, and Limited English Proficiency households — seeking funding for community development, housing, public services, and infrastructure initiatives.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: CDBG and HOME funds allocated countywide for housing and community development activities benefiting low- and moderate-income residents, including: public facilities and infrastructure improvements (33%), housing activities such as acquisition, rehabilitation, and development of owner-occupied and rental housing (42%), public services including homelessness services, emergency shelter operations, eviction prevention, transitional housing, day resource center operations, tenant-based rental assistance, and counseling (15%), economic development, redevelopment of vacant commercial/industrial areas, transportation infrastructure, property acquisition and disposition, down payment assistance, homeowner and renter rehabilitation, affordable housing acquisition and preservation, and program administration. Rental rents must comply with affordability standards (lesser of HUD Fair Market Rent or 30% of 80% AMI gross monthly income for CDBG-funded projects).

It is the policy of Howard County that activities will not be qualified based on service area (LMA) benefit. CDBG Target Areas are identified as neighborhoods with 51% or more of households with incomes below 80% AMI. Geographic restrictions established by Bill No. 18-2014 (June 4, 2014) restrict the construction of housing in Census Tracts and Block Groups if the poverty level is 10% or greater, with the goal of expanding affordable housing opportunities outside of areas of concentration. Areas of concentrated need include Harper's Choice area of northern Columbia (22% poverty rate — highest in county), parts of Ellicott City (10–16% poverty rates), Owen Brown and Long Reach areas around Snowden River Parkway (10–16%), and south Howard County near Laurel (ZIP Code 20723). The Route 1 Corridor is bounded by I-95 to the west, the Anne Arundel County line to the east, MD 100 to the north, and MD 175 to the south. Approximately 94% of the county's subsidized rental units are located in Columbia. Specific development properties referenced include areas in Mt. Airy, Woodbine, Ellicott City (including Burgess Mill Station area and Roger Carter Recreation Center redevelopment), Clarksville, Elkridge, Laurel, and Simpsonville. Regional coordination with the Baltimore Metropolitan Council noted for fair housing activities. No R/ECAPs identified in Howard County.

structured_extraction.program_name: Coordinated Entry System of Homeless Services (CES)
structured_extraction.program_description: The Coordinated Entry System of Homeless Services (CES) connects people experiencing homelessness to housing opportunities in Howard County. It is a required part of the Continuum of Care (CoC) and uses a standardized housing assessment to evaluate each household's vulnerability level. Based on that assessment, individuals, youth, and families are prioritized and referred to shelter, Permanent Supportive Housing, Rapid Rehousing, and Permanent Housing programs based on need rather than first-come, first-served order. The system maintains a By-Name List of all clients seeking housing services, and referrals are made from that list based on vulnerability. The program is managed by Howard County and supported by a network of local service providers, providing a single access point for assessing needs and matching individuals and families to appropriate housing resources. Not all assessed individuals will receive immediate services due to limited resources.
structured_extraction.agency: Howard County Department of Housing and Community Development
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free housing assessment and referral service for people experiencing homelessness. After completing a standardized assessment (takes approximately 15–25 minutes) with a Case Manager, individuals are added to the CES By-Name List and matched to available housing or shelter resources including shelter, Rapid Rehousing, Permanent Supportive Housing, and Permanent Housing programs. Assistance may include rental assistance (variable duration) and Permanent Supportive Housing (PSH). Clients must update their assessment every 90 days to remain active on the By-Name List. Not all assessed individuals will receive immediate services due to limited resources.

structured_extraction.program_name: HUD Approved Monthly Homebuyer Education Workshop
structured_extraction.program_description: Howard County's Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) offers a monthly HUD-approved homebuyer education program for prospective homebuyers interested in purchasing a home in Howard County. The program consists of an 8-hour curriculum: a 6-hour group workshop held one Saturday each month (offered in-person and virtually) and 2 hours of one-on-one counseling scheduled afterward with a credit agency. Topics cover budgeting and credit, financing and mortgage loans, shopping for a home, home inspection, homeowners insurance, the settlement process, downpayment and closing cost resources, and home maintenance. A HUD-certified Housing Counselor facilitates the workshop, supported by volunteer presenters from the real estate industry including a mortgage lender, realtor, home inspector, and title attorney. Completing the program is required for participants in DHCD homeownership assistance programs such as the Settlement Downpayment Loan Program (SDLP) and Moderate Income Housing Unit (MIHU) program.

structured_extraction.program_description: Howard County's MIHU Program is an inclusionary zoning program that requires developers and builders of new housing in certain zoning districts to sell or rent a portion of dwelling units to households of moderate income. The program aims to increase the supply of affordable housing in Howard County and integrate it into all new communities. It serves two main audiences: (1) Developers/builders, who must provide a portion of units at reduced prices or rents for income-qualified households, with MIHU pricing updated twice per year (January 1 and July 1) by the Housing and Community Development Board per Howard County Code Sec. 13.403; and (2) Income-eligible households seeking to purchase or rent affordable units. The Homeownership Program makes below-market-rate new and resale homes available for purchase to moderate-income households (below 80% of Howard County AMI). For-sale unit prices are calculated based on 33% PITI (Principal, Interest, Taxes, Insurance) plus Association Fees and FHA Mortgage Insurance at varying affordability percentages (50–70% depending on unit type). Applications are accepted quarterly in January, April, July, and October through the DHCD online portal. The Rental Program provides reduced-rent apartments in participating communities on a first-come, first-served basis (applications accepted on a rolling basis), targeting households below 60% AMI. Maximum rents are set at 30% of 60% median income with utility allowance deductible. MIHU rental units are set aside in private developments and spread throughout each participating community; residents enjoy the same amenities as market-rate tenants. Lease term is one year minimum with renewal option contingent on annual income recertification; if income exceeds limits at renewal, rent adjusts to market rate rather than eviction. Prevailing interest rates are determined as of December 1 and June 1 each year based on FHA-insured 30-year fixed-rate mortgages in the Baltimore metropolitan area; utility allowances are based on average utility costs for similar sized units in Howard County. Alternative compliance options for developers include a Fee In Lieu payment (per Section 13.402C of the Howard County Code, set yearly by Council resolution), Low Income Housing Units (LIHU) for households below 60% AMI for sale or 40% AMI for rental, and Disability Income Housing Units (DIHU) for rental households at or below 20% AMI who receive disability-based income. A Payment In Lieu of Taxes (PILOT) is available for eligible TOD district projects that designate at least 5% of total units as DIHU and another 15% as a mix of MIHU, LIHU, or DIHU per Council Bill 18-2025; PILOT agreement processing takes 60–90 days for initial review. The current price schedule is effective January 1 through June 30, 2026. Household income limits for the rental program (effective January 1, 2026): 1-person $61,732; 2-person $70,551; 3-person $79,370; 4-person $88,189; 5-person $95,244; 6-person $102,299; 7-person $109,355; 8+ person $116,410. There are 27 participating rental communities located across Howard County (updated March 2026); applicants should call or email to schedule an appointment before visiting. One community (Miller's Grant, Regency Crest) explicitly serves adults 62+.

structured_extraction.program_name: Reinvest Renovate Restore (RRR) Home Rehabilitation Loan Fund Program (Whole Home Housing Repair)
structured_extraction.program_description: Howard County's Reinvest Renovate Restore (RRR) Home Rehabilitation Loan Fund Program — also known as the Rehabilitation Loan Fund (RLF) or Whole Home Housing Repair program — helps income-eligible Howard County homeowners pay for necessary home repairs and improvements that address health, safety, and housing code compliance. Eligible repairs include heating and air conditioning systems, electrical improvements, plumbing, roof replacements, windows and doors, painting, landscaping, bathroom upgrades, energy efficiency improvements, and accessibility modifications such as ramps, chair lifts, and grab bars. The program offers three loan tiers based on household gross annual income relative to Howard County Median Income (HCMI): Tier 1 (at or below 30% HCMI) — 0% interest, no credit score requirement, no monthly payments, with the loan forgiven 20% per year over a 5-year term; Tier 2 (at or below 50% HCMI) — 1% interest, no monthly payments, with deferred repayment due upon sale or transfer of the property; Tier 3 (at or below 80% HCMI) — 2% interest, fully amortizing monthly payments for up to 30 years based on ability to repay. All loans are secured by a Deed of Trust on the property. Grant assistance may also be available for qualifying homeowners. Funds cannot be used for routine cosmetic maintenance only, repaying existing construction work, or repaying outside loans. The program particularly serves low-income seniors and persons with disabilities, helping residents stay safely in their homes through broad home repair and rehabilitation support.

structured_extraction.program_name: Howard County Agricultural Land Preservation Program (ALPP) - Purchased Easements
structured_extraction.program_description: Howard County's Agricultural Land Preservation Program (ALPP) is a voluntary program that protects farmland from development by purchasing perpetual agricultural land preservation easements from willing landowners in Howard County's Rural West. Farmers and agricultural landowners whose land meets certain size and soil criteria may sell a development-restricting easement to the County while retaining ownership and the ability to continue farming. By selling an easement, a landowner permanently gives up the right to develop the land in exchange for compensation, while retaining fee simple title. The easement remains with the land and binds future owners, even if the property is sold. The program has preserved over 23,300 acres in Howard County's Rural West since 1984. The program uses installment purchase agreements (IPAs) that provide semi-annual tax-exempt interest payments and annual principal payments over the contract term. Three IPA options are available: (1) 15-year term with 10% down and 2.50% interest; (2) 20-year term with 10% down and 3.00% interest; (3) 20-year term with 15% down and 1.00% interest. The county pays up to $40,000 per acre (formula adopted July 6, 2020 as County Council Resolution 36-2020). The program is funded by a dedicated 20% portion of the County's 1.25% local transfer tax. Property owners with ALPP easements also receive a property tax credit equal to 75% of the County property tax on the land (excluding improvements); new participants must apply for the tax credit by April 1 preceding the new tax year, after which it renews automatically. A non-refundable $200 application fee (payable to Howard County Director of Finance) is required. The Agricultural Preservation Board reviews applications and makes recommendations to the County Executive. The program aims to preserve Howard County's agricultural heritage and open space.

The county pays up to $40,000 per acre at fair market value (pricing formula adopted July 6, 2020 as County Council Resolution 36-2020). Payments are disbursed as semi-annual tax-exempt interest and annual principal payments over the contract term. The landowner retains fee simple ownership and the ability to farm. The program is funded by a dedicated 20% portion of the County's 1.25% local transfer tax. Additionally, property owners with ALPP easements receive a property tax credit equal to 75% of the County property tax on the land (excluding improvements). New participants must apply for the tax credit by April 1 preceding the new tax year; thereafter it renews automatically. A non-refundable $200 application fee (payable to Howard County Director of Finance) is required.

structured_extraction.program_name: Howard County Historic Property Tax Credit Programs
structured_extraction.program_description: Howard County offers property tax credit programs that provide financial incentives for owners of designated historic properties to restore, rehabilitate, or preserve those structures. The program is administered through the Historic Preservation Commission (HPC) and the Howard County Department of Planning and Zoning. Two local credits are available: a 25% tax credit on qualifying rehabilitation, restoration, or preservation costs, and an assessment-based tax credit on historic or heritage property improvements. Properties listed on the Howard County Historic Sites Inventory (over 1,000 properties) or located within local historic districts such as Ellicott City and Lawyers Hill are eligible. Applicants must obtain pre-approval from the HPC before beginning qualifying work and final approval upon completion. State and federal historic tax credits are also available through separate programs.

structured_extraction.program_name: Agricultural Grant for Innovation and Expansion (AGIE)
structured_extraction.program_description: Howard County's Agricultural Grant for Innovation and Expansion (AGIE) is a competitive grant program administered by the Howard County Economic Development Authority (HCEDA) in cooperation with the Howard County Office of Agriculture (OOAG) that helps Howard County agricultural producers expand or diversify their business operations. Since launching in 2012, the program has provided nearly $500,000 in direct support to local farmers through 73 individual grants. Eligible applicants include crop or livestock producers or processors, agricultural cooperatives, seafood processors, and primary or secondary timber products processors. Eligible activities include research and development, construction of production buildings, major fixtures, and processing facilities, as well as other investments that facilitate expansion, sustainability, or education of Howard County agriculture. There is one annual grant cycle per year (running August through June), with individual awards ranging from $1,000 to $20,000 and a total annual budget of $100,000. An organization or farm can only receive one grant (EAG or AGIE) per cycle. First-time applicants receive a 10-point scoring bonus. Applications are scored out of 200 points by a panel selected by HCEDA, and awards are announced approximately three weeks after the deadline (by March 10, 2026 for the FY26 cycle). The full value of the grant must be spent by July 31, 2027.

Total annual funding is $100,000 (e.g., six grants totaling $100,000 were awarded in 2024). One annual grant cycle per year (August through June); an organization or farm can only receive one grant (EAG or AGIE) per cycle. structured_extraction.program_description: The Eastern Howard County Enterprise Zone offers tax credits and tax benefits to businesses located along the Route 1 corridor and in Columbia Gateway. Businesses can receive a local property tax credit on new investment in commercial and industrial improvements, and a state income tax credit for hiring new employees. The zone covers 2,337 acres of commercial and industrial properties along Route 1 and the 1,000-acre Columbia Gateway business park. The designation was approved on December 15, 2024 and expires December 14, 2034.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Two main benefits: (1) Local Property Tax Benefit — a 10-year property tax credit on the increased assessed value resulting from qualifying commercial or industrial improvements. Credit starts at 80% for the first five years, then declines by 10 percentage points each year for the following five years. The state reimburses counties 50% of lost property tax revenue from the increased assessment. Residential and government-owned properties are not eligible. (2) State Income Tax Credit — a one-time credit of $1,000 per new full-time employee hired in the zone, enhanced to up to $6,000 total over three tax years for each economically disadvantaged employee hired.

Some additional parcels north of MD 175 adjacent to MD 108 are also included. Must be within existing State Priority Funding Area.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Howard County Enhanced Agricultural Grant (EAG) Pilot Program provides funding to farmers, non-profits, organizations, individuals, and government entities supporting Howard County agriculture. The program empowers, preserves, and supports agriculture and agriculture-supporting organizations through programming, research, equipment purchases, educational programming, and capital investments that facilitate the expansion, sustainability, and education of Howard County agriculture. Funding comes from the Howard County Agricultural Preservation Fund, with a total available funding pool of $500,000 per cycle distributed among multiple recipients. Grants are offered once a year, with optional additional offerings at the discretion of the Office of Community Sustainability (OCS) and the Agricultural Preservation Board (APB). The program is administered by the Howard County Economic Development Authority (HCEDA) in partnership with the Howard County Office of Community Sustainability and the Agricultural Preservation Board. Current cycle awards range from $20,000 to $250,000 per applicant, with typical awards between $20,000 and $70,000. Past awards in the 2023 pilot program ranged from approximately $19,854 to $64,716 per recipient. EAG awardees initially receive 20% of the award, with the balance reimbursed upon submission of receipts and reimbursement forms. Applicants that have never received an EAG or AGIE grant receive a 10-point bonus during scoring.

EAG awardees initially receive 20% of the award, with the balance reimbursed upon submission of receipts and reimbursement forms. Only one grant (EAG or AGIE) may be awarded per organization or farm per cycle. Applicants that have never received an EAG or AGIE grant receive a 10-point bonus during scoring. structured_extraction.program_description: The Emergency Food and Shelter Program (EFSP) is a federally funded program established in 1983 that provides grants to local nonprofit and government organizations to supplement and expand emergency food and shelter services for people in need. A Local Board in Howard County reviews community needs, accepts applications from local organizations, and allocates grant funds to selected Local Recipient Organizations (LROs). The program gives special emphasis to serving the elderly, families with children, Native Americans, veterans, people with disabilities, and homeless or formerly homeless individuals. Funding is distributed in phases (funding cycles), with historical allocations documented in phase-specific summaries.
structured_extraction.agency: Howard County Emergency Food and Shelter Program Local Board
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Federal grant funds are allocated to Local Recipient Organizations (LROs) to provide emergency food and shelter services. Spending priorities include: (1) Rental Assistance (up to 90 days/3 months per client per phase; up to 3 months mortgage assistance); (2) Food Assistance/Served Meals ($3 per meal); (3) Mass Shelter ($12.50 per diem/night). Other eligible uses include utility assistance, other shelter (hotel/motel), supplies/equipment, and repairs/code compliance. The Local Board reviews applications and distributes funds each phase (funding cycle). Historical allocations are documented in phase-specific summaries (e.g., Phase 41, Phase 40, Phase 39, Phase ARPA-R, Phase 38, Phase 37, Phase CARES).

structured_extraction.program_description: The Citizens' Election Fund is Howard County's public campaign financing program that provides matching county funds to candidates running for County Council or County Executive. Created to reduce the influence of large private campaign contributions, the program encourages candidates to accept small individual qualifying donations instead of large contributions. Certified candidates who opt into the program and decline large private donations receive matching public funds for qualifying small contributions. The county allocates funds to support the program (e.g., $2M appropriation for the 2019–2022 cycle; $680,000 approved in May 2025). The Citizens' Election Fund Commission oversees the process and reviews compliance, and participating candidates submit matching fund reports per the reporting timeline through the Maryland Campaign Reporting Information System (MD CRIS) or MD FOCUS. A Lunch and Learn training series is available to help campaign finance teams understand the process and program requirements. The program is authorized under Section 10-300 of the Howard County Municipal Code.

structured_extraction.assistance_description: Matching county funds are provided to Maryland State Board of Elections-certified candidates for County Council and County Executive who participate in the program by declining large private contributions and instead raising small qualifying donations. The County Council allocates varying amounts to the fund by election cycle (e.g., $2M appropriation for the 2019–2022 cycle; $680,000 approved in May 2025). For the 2019–2022 cycle, $914,700 was disbursed to candidates from a combined appropriation and citizen donation pool. Candidates must be certified by the Maryland State Board of Elections and agree to turn down large private donations in exchange for access to matching funds. Matching fund reports are submitted through the Maryland Campaign Reporting Information System (MD CRIS) or MD FOCUS per the established reporting timeline.

structured_extraction.program_description: Howard County Government partners with nonprofits to meet basic needs and foster safety, security, and well-being for Howard County residents. The program, operated by the Howard County Office of Community Partnerships, offers three grant types: Core Support Grants (funding for both organization operations and direct service delivery), Human Service Transportation (HST) Program Grants (funding transportation services for adults with disabilities), and One-Time Project Grants (funding for specific, time-sensitive projects that address emerging needs or opportunities affecting critical human services). Funding focuses on two levels: Level I (Basic Human Needs) covering Hunger Relief and Nutrition, Homeless System Services, Health Services including Mental and Behavioral Health, and Reliable and Affordable Access to Resources for Basic Human Needs; and Level II (Safety & Security) covering Personal Security and Safety, Safe and Stable Housing, Legal Assistance, Job Skills and Employment, Healthy Aging, Family and Community Resiliency, and Reliable and Affordable Access to Resources Related to Safety and Security. The program is listed as an assistance and referral resource under the Department of Community Resources and Services.

structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants are awarded through the county budgeting process. Five grant categories have been awarded in FY26 (total $8,313,625): (1) Core Support Grants for both organization operations and direct service delivery (applicant must be in operation at least 3 years); (2) Human Service Transportation (HST) Program Grants for transportation services for adults with disabilities; (3) One-Time Project Grants (Emerging Needs & Opportunities) for specific, time-sensitive projects addressing emerging human service needs; (4) Safety, Security & Well-being (SSW) Program Awards; and (5) Initiative Grant Awards. Grant amounts are subject to change from year to year based on available budget resources. Funding is dependent upon resources available each budget year.

structured_extraction.program_description: Howard County Health Department, in partnership with the Howard County Library System, provides free gun safety locks to adults at all county library locations. The program aims to increase gun safety, reduce accidental injuries, and help prevent firearm suicide by creating a critical pause in moments of crisis. Gun locks are available at the library front desk during normal business hours — no library card or proof of residency is required. Initial locks were provided courtesy of the VA Maryland Health Care System; future locks are funded through a Maryland Department of Health grant.

No library card or proof of residency is required. Visitors simply ask at the front desk and provide basic demographic information for Health Department use. The program also provides educational resources and guidance on safe firearm storage (cable locks, lockboxes, safes), storing ammunition separately, and removing firearms during mental health crises for suicide prevention. Initial locks were provided courtesy of the VA Maryland Health Care System; future locks will be funded through a Maryland Department of Health grant.

structured_extraction.program_description: The P.E.A.C.E. structured_extraction.program_description: The Howard County Health Department's PrEP Program provides HIV prevention services to help HIV-negative individuals reduce their risk of getting HIV. The program offers access to PrEP medications (daily pills such as Truvada/generic Truvada, Descovy, or Yeztugo, or long-acting injections such as Apretude), HIV and STI testing, medication distribution, care coordination, and referrals to additional services such as housing, transportation, health insurance, and employment support. A dedicated PrEP Navigator helps clients navigate insurance coverage, financial assistance programs, and medication access to ensure cost is never a barrier — including assistance with copays, coinsurance, and deductibles. For uninsured clients, patient assistance programs may cover the full cost of PrEP. The program is open to everyone regardless of residency, immigration status, or insurance status.

structured_extraction.program_description: Howard County offers free naloxone (Narcan) training and distribution to Howard County residents through multiple channels. structured_extraction.program_name: Howard County Child Care Resource Center
structured_extraction.program_description: The Howard County Child Care Resource Center (CCRC), operated by the Howard County Office of Children and Families, provides free technical assistance, training workshops, referral services, and access to a resource room to current and prospective child care providers, early childhood professionals, and parents in Howard County. A Technical Assistance Specialist offers one-on-one advice and guidance covering program improvement (Maryland EXCELS, accreditation, environmental rating scales), infant and toddler care, professional development planning, licensing and regulatory compliance, equipment selection, space arrangement, marketing, staff management, and behavior/special needs strategies. The Center also supports individuals seeking to become registered family child care providers and offers infant and early childhood mental health consultation for child care providers working with young children who have disruptive behavior. Monthly training workshops are held at 9830 Patuxent Woods Drive, Columbia, MD, in both in-person and online (WebEx) formats on a pre-registration basis, covering required child care licensing topics such as CPR, medication administration, and health/safety. Monthly workshops on child development, health/safety, curriculum, social-emotional learning, special needs, and professionalism are offered at $5 per course (2–3 hours). On-site training at provider locations is available for groups of 10 or more staff. The Resource Room (open Monday–Friday, 8:30 a.m.–4:45 p.m.) offers a lending library of books and resources on child development topics, as well as laminating, copying, die cuts, computers, and book binding services. Child care referrals for parents are available through LOCATE: Child Care at 877-261-0060. Some courses have prerequisites (e.g., NAFCC accreditation prerequisites, DAP knowledge, ADA compliance requirements).

The program supports evidence-based prevention, treatment, recovery, and harm reduction initiatives to supplement existing resources and expand services that reduce the harm caused by the opioid crisis. structured_extraction.program_name: The Loan Closet of Howard County
structured_extraction.program_description: The Loan Closet of Howard County is a durable medical equipment (DME) re-use and education program operated by the Howard County Office of Disability Services. It collects donated durable medical equipment and assistive technology from residents who no longer need it and redistributes it at no cost to Howard County residents who need wheelchairs, walkers, shower chairs, crutches, toileting aids, bathing aids, lifts, gait belts, reachers, dressing aids, canes, and other assistive devices due to injury, illness, or medical condition. The program serves residents of any age—from youth to end of life—regardless of insurance status, including uninsured residents and those whose insurance will not cover or has delayed approval of needed equipment. Equipment is available for free short-term loan; certain high-demand items (wheelchairs, GeriChairs, Sit-to-Stand Lifts, mechanical lifts, U-Step Walkers) are subject to a 90-day loan time limit. A healthcare provider referral is required to receive equipment. The program also provides education and instructions on how to safely size, operate, and adjust equipment. Equipment pickup takes place by appointment at the Loan Closet location in Columbia, MD.

Certain high-demand items (wheelchairs, GeriChairs, Sit-to-Stand Lifts, mechanical lifts, U-Step Walkers) are subject to a 90-day loan time limit. structured_extraction.program_description: Howard County's Apprenticeship Opportunity Program (AOP) provides financial incentives to eligible businesses and nonprofits that create, reactivate, or enhance a registered apprenticeship program. Employers can receive $5,000 per apprentice hired, up to $20,000 per employer, to offset startup costs such as recruitment, training and related instruction, onboarding, mentoring, tools, gear, and uniforms. The program focuses on growing apprenticeships in high-demand industries like electrical, education, and healthcare, and encourages employers to develop a skilled local workforce. Funding is limited and available on a first-come, first-served basis. In 2024–2025, the program awarded $285,000 in total incentives supporting 26 active apprenticeship sponsors and 57 new registered apprentices.

structured_extraction.program_name: Howard County Summer Youth Employment Program
structured_extraction.program_description: A six-week paid summer work experience program that connects Howard County youth (ages 14–24) with worksites related to their career interests and career development opportunities. Staff work one-on-one with participants to place them at worksites aligned with their career goals. The program runs approximately July 1 through August 7 and is capped at approximately 350 participants per year. Priority is given to youth facing significant barriers, including those with a 504 plan or Individualized Education Plan (IEP), youth in foster care, pregnant or parenting youth, English Language Learners, economically disadvantaged youth, and those navigating other significant barriers. Howard County Government pays participants via direct deposit; no paper checks are issued. Each youth may participate for a maximum of two years, and only two youth from the same household may participate at the same time. The program also includes broader workforce development services such as career exploration, job skills training, tutoring, resume assistance, interview preparation, and job search support.

The program helps older adults and people with disabilities connect to health and supportive services, providing trained counselors who help people explore care options and community resources tailored to their needs. Services include guidance on financial benefits, healthcare programs (including Medicare/health insurance counseling), housing options, caregiver support, wellness programs, social day programs, and 50+ Center access. structured_extraction.program_description: The IRC Center for Economic Opportunity (CEO) offers fixed-rate installment auto loans to help individuals finance the purchase of a vehicle. Loans are available up to $20,000 with terms up to 72 months. Base interest rates range from 9.99% to 11.99% depending on state, with discounts available for Fresh Start program participants (-1%), higher FICO scores (up to -2%), and larger down payments (up to -2%), resulting in effective rates as low as 5.99%. A 2% closing fee applies. There are no late fees, insufficient funds fees, or prepayment penalties. Applicants work with a financial counselor, submit an application through the Happy Mango platform, and receive a pre-approval decision from the CEO underwriting team. Approved funds are sent directly to the vehicle seller via ACH or certified check. Borrowers receive a one-month grace period before the first payment is due, and monthly payments are automatically deducted.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: 1. Visit a local partner office or consult a financial counselor to complete a CEO Loan Application. Bring a government-issued photo ID, personal email address, a U.S. checking bank account with routing/account number, two most recent monthly bank statements, and two most recent pay stubs or income statements. 2. Submit the application through the Happy Mango platform. The CEO underwriting team reviews the application and may request additional documentation. Loan decisions are typically made within three weeks. 3. If approved, accept the pre-approval offer and link a bank account on Happy Mango. structured_extraction.program_name: IRC Center for Economic Opportunity (CEO) Lending Program
structured_extraction.program_description: The International Rescue Committee's Center for Economic Opportunity (IRC-CEO) is a nonprofit Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) loan fund that provides fair, responsible, and flexible loans to refugees, immigrants, newcomers to the U.S., and low-income families who are often excluded from the traditional financial system. As a special purpose credit program, applicants must be referred through a community partner organization. CEO takes a holistic approach to lending, working with borrowers and community partners to help people build credit, achieve financial stability, and access opportunities. Loan products include: Credit Building Ladder Loans ($100–$1,000, 0% interest, 6–20 month terms), Auto Purchase Loans (up to $20,000, 5.99%–11.99%, up to 72 months), Auto Refinance Loans (up to $20,000, 6.99%–11.99%, up to 72 months), Education and Training Loans (up to $8,000, 3.99%–4.99%, up to 60 months), Business/Microenterprise Loans (up to $50,000, 0%–11.99%, up to 72 months), Digital Accelerator Loans (up to $2,500, 0%–1.99%, up to 24 months), Immigration Loans (up to $8,000, 4.99%–6.99%, up to 60 months), and Personal Loans (up to $2,500, 7.99%–13.99%, up to 48 months). Fee-based (no-interest) alternatives are available for those with religious or moral objections to interest. Borrowers also receive financial education to help them understand and manage their credit. The program also offers incentivized savings accounts and integrated financial coaching services. The program reports a 94% repayment rate on consumer and business loans, and over $47 million in assets (homes, cars, businesses) purchased by program participants. The program operates across 25 states plus Washington D.C., including Maryland, where IRC Baltimore, IRC Silver Spring, and Civic Works (Baltimore) serve as community partners.
structured_extraction.agency: International Rescue Committee — Center for Economic Opportunity (IRC-CEO)
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Fixed-rate installment loans across multiple product types with amounts ranging from $100 up to $50,000 and terms up to 72 months. Consumer loans include: Credit Building Ladder ($100–$1,000, 0% interest, 6–20 month terms), Education and Training (up to $8,000, 3.99%–4.99%, up to 60 months), Immigration (up to $8,000, 4.99%–6.99%, up to 60 months), Personal (up to $2,500, 7.99%–13.99%, up to 48 months), Auto Purchase (up to $20,000, 5.99%–11.99%, up to 72 months), and Auto Refinance (up to $20,000, 6.99%–11.99%, up to 72 months). Business loans include: Microenterprise (up to $50,000, 0%–11.99%, up to 72 months) and Digital Accelerator (up to $2,500, 0%–1.99%, up to 24 months). Fee-based (no-interest) alternatives are available. Technical assistance is provided for business/microenterprise borrowers. Financial education is provided alongside all loans to help borrowers understand and manage their credit. The program also offers incentivized savings accounts and integrated financial coaching services. Not all loan products are available in all states; local partners can advise on available products.

Applicants must be enrolled in and referred by a community partner organization such as IRC Baltimore, IRC Silver Spring, or Civic Works (Baltimore).
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Credit building, vehicle purchase or refinance, vocational training or education, business startup and development costs, digital business acceleration, immigration process fees, personal expenses such as computers or car repairs, work-related expenses, and emergencies. Funds help borrowers establish credit histories and achieve financial stability.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available in Maryland and 25 other states plus Washington D.C. Maryland partners include IRC Baltimore, IRC Silver Spring, and Civic Works (Baltimore, MD). Not all loan products are available in all states; consult local partner for available products. California loans are made under a California Financing Law license; Arizona loans are made under an Arizona Consumer Lender license; Michigan loans are capped at 11% APR.

structured_extraction.program_name: Graduate Fellowship for Entrepreneurship in Medicine (GEM)
structured_extraction.program_description: A two-year, cohort-based fellowship for Johns Hopkins PhD and MD/PhD students that provides financial support, commercialization training, mentorship, and networking to help scientists turn research into real-world impact through startups, licensing, policy, or translational research.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Two years of salary coverage, travel support, tuition for business courses, curated programming, and an additional stipend. Monthly commercialization training sessions led by venture capitalists, entrepreneurs, and industry leaders. One-on-one mentorship from founders, investors, and faculty. Access to conferences, VC introductions, and premier events including the JHTV Innovation Summit and BIO International.
structured_extraction.program_audience: 2nd year or later PhD or MD/PhD students at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine who are focused on innovation through startups, policy, licensing, or translational research.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Salary, travel, business course tuition, programming, and additional stipend for fellows during the two-year fellowship period.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Open to PhD and MD/PhD students enrolled at the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine.
requirements_list: Must be a 2nd year or later PhD or MD/PhD student at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine
Focus on innovation through startups, policy, licensing, or translational research
Submit CV or resume
Submit 1-page research summary
Submit 1-page personal statement explaining interest in the fellowship
Submit letter of support from PI or research advisor
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Submit an online application form with demographic and short-answer questions, along with a CV/resume, 1-page research summary, 1-page personal statement, and a letter of support from your PI or research advisor.

structured_extraction.program_description: Hexcite is a 16-week AI and digital health venture lab run by Johns Hopkins Technology Ventures (JHTV). Johns Hopkins innovators — including faculty, clinicians, students, and local entrepreneurs — transform digital health ideas into fundable startups through customer discovery, AI-powered prototyping, and team building. Weekly workshops cover commercialization, business modeling, IP, product planning, and pitch development. At the end of the program, a select project receives a $10,000 award. The program has two tracks: an Idea Track for those with a digital health idea, and an Operator Track for those who bring skills to execute on an idea.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: A 16-week cohort program providing workshops, mentorship, team building, and resources to develop a digital health startup. Upon completion, a select project is awarded $10,000 to accelerate early traction.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Applications are currently closed for the 2026 cohort
structured_extraction.program_audience: Faculty, clinicians, staff, graduate students, postdocs from Johns Hopkins University or Johns Hopkins Health System, JHU alumni, and local entrepreneurs with digital health ideas or relevant skills.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Customer discovery, AI-powered prototyping, team building, pitch development, and early startup traction. The $10,000 award is intended to accelerate and build early traction for a selected project.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Program is based at the East Baltimore Campus of Johns Hopkins University. Participants must attend in-person sessions.
requirements_list: Must be faculty, clinician, staff, graduate student, postdoc from JHU or JHHS, JHU alumni, or local entrepreneur
Idea Track: must have a digital health idea or project
Operator Track: must bring diverse skills (technical, design, or business) in digital health
Attend in-person afternoon sessions at East Baltimore Campus
Dedicate 10-20+ hours per week for 16 weeks
Present at the final showcase event
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Applicants submit their digital health idea or skills profile. JHTV evaluates applicants and selects the cohort. Idea Track participants are matched with Operator Track participants who need teams. Six Idea Track participants are accepted per cohort.

structured_extraction.program_description: The I-Corps program is an immersive entrepreneurial training program developed by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and offered at no cost by Johns Hopkins Technology Ventures. Researchers, faculty, students, and community entrepreneurs participate in customer discovery research to learn how to take their innovations from idea to market. Each cohort runs over a 4-week period and includes instructor-led training, mentorship from established entrepreneurs, and networking opportunities.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free 4-week cohort-based entrepreneurial training program. Participants identify customer segments, conduct customer interviews, learn to articulate a value proposition, receive instructor-led training, and gain mentorship from established entrepreneurs. Offered multiple times per year at no cost.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Researchers, faculty, students, and community entrepreneurs looking to commercialize innovations, particularly in life sciences.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Entrepreneurial training including customer discovery, business model development, value proposition design, and market exploration.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Open to faculty and innovators from across the Mid-Atlantic I-Corps Hub and partner organizations. Sessions are primarily virtual with an in-person networking event in Baltimore.
requirements_list: Completion of a short I-Corps Prep course required prior to participation
Applicants must be researchers, faculty, students, or community entrepreneurs with an innovation to commercialize
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply via the Mid-Atlantic I-Corps online application. Complete the I-Corps Prep course by the deadline. Teams are grouped into tracks (digital health, therapeutics, medical devices and diagnostics, biotech) and participate in virtual sessions plus one in-person networking event.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Innovator in Residence (IIR) Program connects Johns Hopkins faculty and student innovators with experienced life sciences industry leaders who provide mentorship and guidance on early translational research, entrepreneurship, product development, company creation, and financing strategies. The program supports high-level innovation projects through in-person visits, virtual office hours, and educational sessions such as workshops, bootcamps, and panels.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Participants receive ad-hoc mentorship and guidance from an experienced industry leader (Innovator in Residence) who visits Baltimore two to four times a year for meetings and educational sessions, hosts monthly virtual office hours for faculty, and provides advice on product development strategy, company creation, partnership formation, financing, and investor preparation.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Johns Hopkins University faculty and student innovators interested in life sciences entrepreneurship and translational research, as well as Johns Hopkins-affiliated industry leaders interested in sharing expertise.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Not applicable — this is a mentorship and technical assistance program, not a funding program.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to Johns Hopkins University faculty and students, primarily based in Baltimore.
requirements_list: Must be affiliated with Johns Hopkins University as a faculty member or student
Primary focus on therapeutics and life sciences innovation
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Johns Hopkins innovators interested in connecting with the Innovator in Residence should contact Christina DeMur (christina.demur@jhu.edu), director of technology development at JHTV. Industry leaders interested in serving as an Innovator in Residence should contact Allison Wiles (arhwiles@jhu.edu), director of innovation initiatives at JHTV.

structured_extraction.program_description: A two-year paid fellowship program run by Johns Hopkins Technology Ventures for current Johns Hopkins full-time students, training them in technology commercialization and entrepreneurship. Fellows work 8–10 hours per week during the academic year with a full-time summer option, gaining hands-on experience in technology development, technology transfer, and corporate partnerships. Students with technical or scientific backgrounds learn how to bring research and innovations to market, supported by mentorship from experienced commercialization professionals. Applications are submitted through the SMILE portal.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: A two-year paid fellowship providing stipend compensation for approximately 8–10 hours of work per week during the academic year, with the option to work full-time over the summer. Fellows receive structured training in technology commercialization and personal mentorship from senior commercialization professionals. Students apply through the SMILE portal (studentjob.jh.edu), position 12144.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Current Johns Hopkins undergraduate, master's, and PhD students who are U.S. citizens or permanent residents, preferably with a technical or scientific background, who are interested in commercialization and entrepreneurship.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Fellowship stipend supporting students working on technology development, technology transfer, and corporate partnership projects at JHTV; training and education in technology commercialization.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Open to full-time students currently enrolled at Johns Hopkins University.
requirements_list: Must be a Johns Hopkins University full-time student (undergraduate, master's, or PhD candidate)
Must be a U.S. Citizen or permanent resident
Technical/scientific background preferred (e.g., biology, physics, chemistry, computer science, engineering)
School of Medicine PhD students require PI and departmental approval
Highly competitive selection process
Curiosity, team orientation, and ability to understand complex technologies required
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply through the SMILE portal (studentjob.jh.edu), position 12144. Applications close May 3, 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Additional details available at the Application Information page on the JHTV website. Contact Anna Gonye for more information.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Johns Hopkins University President's Innovation Award is given annually to one innovative early-to-mid career faculty member who is focused on translating research beyond academia into real-world products or services. The $250,000 award supports recipients during the crucial early years of their careers, giving them freedom to invest in activities most likely to advance their innovations toward the marketplace.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: A single $250,000 award given to one recipient per year. The award does not require a specific business idea or technology development proposal — it is an investment in an investigator's career and translational goals broadly. Funds can be used for key or exploratory experiments, lab support, conference attendance, CRO work, publication of findings, etc.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Full-time tenure-track (or equivalent) Johns Hopkins faculty members, especially at the Assistant or Associate Professor stage, who have demonstrated a commitment to translating science into real-world products or services.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Key or exploratory experiments, lab support, conference attendance, CRO work, publication of findings, or other activities that advance commercialization of scientific discoveries.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Nominees must be full-time faculty at Johns Hopkins University.
requirements_list: Nominee must be a full-time tenure-track (or equivalent) JHU faculty member
Nominee must have demonstrated a commitment to translating science into real-world products or services
Early or mid-career stage (Assistant or Associate Professor) preferred
Nomination submitted by any full-time JHU faculty member

Nomination package includes: nominator contact info, nominee contact info, nominee CV, letter of nomination (up to 3 pages), one-page summary of research and planned use of funds, and a sample work product
Finalists must submit a letter of support from a Dean or Department Chair
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Any full-time JHU faculty member may nominate an eligible colleague. Submissions are reviewed in two tiers: the first tier narrows candidates from initial nominations; finalists are then asked for a letter of support from a Dean or Department Chair. Finalist packages are forwarded to the JHU president and provost for final selection. Winner is announced in late March.

structured_extraction.program_description: Johns Hopkins Technology Ventures (JHTV) offers non-dilutive translational funding twice per year to help Johns Hopkins faculty and researchers advance early-stage innovations toward commercialization. A single application provides access to three funds: the Cohen Translational Engineering Fund (for Whiting School of Engineering faculty), the Louis B. Thalheimer Fund for Translational Research (for proof-of-concept and validation studies across Johns Hopkins), and the Zizic Translational Fund (for translational research university-wide, with a focus on biomedicine). The Thalheimer and Zizic funds are evergreen — when funded technologies are successfully licensed, a portion of license revenue (twice the award amount) is repaid to the fund to support future projects. Awards are flexible based on project needs, typically capped at $50,000, and support ongoing technology development across life sciences, devices, energy, and software/digital sectors. The program encourages a phased development approach, with faculty able to apply at multiple stages of their project. Proposals are evaluated on innovation, scientific merit, market impact, technical feasibility, and commercialization potential, with finalists presenting in person to the JHTV team. Eligible expenses include in vivo efficacy studies, formulation optimization, animal studies, materials and reagents, analytical services, and regulatory consulting; faculty salary and indirect costs are excluded.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Non-dilutive grant funding provided twice per year through a single application process that routes applicants to one or more of three funds (Cohen, Thalheimer, Zizic). Awards are flexible based on project needs, typically capped at $50,000, with project periods of approximately 3–9 months. Funding supports proof-of-concept work, prototype development, and commercialization readiness activities to de-risk technologies and enhance their commercial value. Eligible expenses include in vivo efficacy studies, formulation optimization, animal studies, materials and reagents, analytical services, and regulatory consulting. Faculty salary and indirect costs are excluded.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Johns Hopkins University faculty, postdocs, and researchers with formally disclosed early-stage translational technologies seeking funding to advance toward commercialization
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Proof-of-concept studies, prototype development, and commercialization readiness activities to de-risk technologies and enhance their commercial value; in vivo efficacy studies and formulation optimization; animal studies, materials and reagents, analytical services, and regulatory consulting; IND-enabling data and regulatory strategy development; technology development structured as a phased development plan to reach key milestones. Faculty salary and indirect costs are not eligible.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Applicants must have a full, joint, or courtesy faculty appointment at Johns Hopkins University
requirements_list: Must be affiliated with Johns Hopkins University
At least one investigator must have a full, joint, or courtesy faculty appointment at Johns Hopkins University
Technology must be formally disclosed to JHTV and assigned a case number
Invention must not be subject to any pre-existing exclusive licenses, non-exclusive licenses, or options
Cohen Fund applicants must be Whiting School of Engineering faculty
Zizic Fund focuses on biomedical and other breakthrough innovations university-wide
Only one application per Lead Principal Investigator per application cycle
Application must use the non-confidential pitch deck format provided by JHTV
Deck must include a concise, business-focused narrative with graphics addressing unmet need, solution, team, preliminary data, IP, competitive landscape, and commercialization potential
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Prepare a non-confidential pitch deck using the provided template and submit via the online application portal. Applications open March 23, 2026 and close April 14, 2026. Finalists are notified and collaborate with JHTV to refine their presentation for an in-person pitch. Pre-application support is available from the Technology Development team. An information session recording is available on the program page. Next cycle opens September 2026.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Venture Mentorship Program (VMP) provides business-focused group mentorship to Johns Hopkins faculty, students, and startups. Groups of two to four volunteer mentors guide assigned ventures through the commercialization process over the course of multiple months. The program uses a structured model adapted from MIT and focuses on the business aspects of launching a startup.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free group mentorship from two to four volunteer mentors who guide ventures through the commercialization process over multiple months. Mentors focus on the business aspects of the startup. The VMP office handles all administrative work including applications and scheduling.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Johns Hopkins faculty, students, and startups (including early-stage) from all nine Johns Hopkins schools
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Business mentorship and guidance through the commercialization process
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Open to Johns Hopkins faculty, students, and startups affiliated with Johns Hopkins University
requirements_list: Must be a Johns Hopkins faculty member, student, or startup
Both mentors and mentees must apply to participate
Mentors must sign a statement of guiding principles/code of ethics
Free to mentees; mentors are unpaid volunteers
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply via the VMP office, which handles all administrative work including applications and scheduling. Contact vmp@jh.edu for more information or to apply.

structured_extraction.program_description: A five-year, universitywide grant initiative launched in 2025 to seed and sustain community-academic partnerships addressing local community needs. The fund offers two grant streams: (1) Institute, Center, and Program Grants of up to $100,000 for JHU institutes, centers, and programs with a history of community-based academic engagement; and (2) Community-Based Project and Research Grants of up to $30,000 or $80,000 for JHU faculty collaborating with community partners on projects or research.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Two grant streams are available. (1) Institute, Center, and Program Grants: up to $100,000 per award over a term of up to two years to support community-based academic engagement at JHU institutes, centers, or programs. (2) Community-Based Project and Research Grants: up to $30,000 for established partnerships (at least one year old) or up to $80,000 for firmly established partnerships (at least two years old), each over a term of up to two years. Funds may be used for salary (including fringe), graduate and undergraduate students, postdoctoral fellows, equipment, supplies, travel, and events. For Project/Research Grants, at least half the budget should go to the community partner or direct community benefit.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Applications for the 2026-2027 cycle have closed. Applications for the 2027-2028 cycle will open in Fall 2026.
structured_extraction.program_audience: JHU faculty (tenure-track and tenured), staff and faculty in leadership roles at JHU institutes/centers/programs, and their community partners working on local community-engaged projects and research.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Salary (including fringe), graduate students, undergraduate students, postdoctoral fellows or technicians, supplies, equipment, travel, events, and community partner activities/services.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Primarily Greater Baltimore and Washington, D.C., but proposals from any geographic location where JHU is embedded in local communities are welcome.
requirements_list: Institute, Center, and Program Grants: applicants must be staff or faculty in leadership positions at institutes, centers, or programs with a history of community-based academic engagement.
Institute, Center, and Program Grants: the entity must employ at least one FTE (not the applicant) who dedicates at least 75% of their effort to that institute/center/program.
Institute, Center, and Program Grants: each institute, center, or program may submit only one application; individual applicants may submit up to two applications on behalf of different entities.
Institute, Center, and Program Grants: all staff/faculty leads must be full-time at JHU.
Community-Based Project and Research Grants: must be led by a JHU tenure-track or tenured faculty member from an eligible school/division.
Community-Based Project and Research Grants: must include at least one (and no more than three) named community partners.
Community-Based Project and Research Grants: only one Project/Research proposal per lead PI is accepted per cycle.
Community-Based Project and Research Grants: partnerships must have existed for at least one year to be eligible for the up-to-$30,000 tier, and at least two years for the up-to-$80,000 tier.
Post-award: recipients must submit a mid-term progress report and complete an end-of-term survey; they may also be asked to present at an annual JHU Community-Academic Partnerships Symposium.
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Applications are submitted through a JHU application portal. Institute, Center, and Program Grant applications require a title, a proposal (up to three pages covering six sections), and a budget with justification. Community-Based Project and Research Grant applications require a title, abstract, proposal (up to three pages), budget, CVs/biosketches for all leads, a letter of affirmation from each community partner, and up to five keywords. All components for Project/Research Grants must be combined into a single PDF upload. Award decisions are announced in Spring; funds are made available starting in late Spring.

structured_extraction.program_name: Johns Hopkins Live Near Your Work
structured_extraction.program_description: Johns Hopkins University helps its employees purchase homes in Baltimore City by providing financial assistance through the Live Near Your Work program. Since 2009, the program has given over $10 million to more than 1,500 employees to buy homes in Baltimore. The program offers up to $17,000 in down payment and closing cost assistance for eligible employees purchasing a home in qualifying Healthy Neighborhoods, including Remington, Better Waverly, Waverly, Bayview, Highlandtown, Patterson Park, Ednor Gardens, Charles North, Mount Vernon, and Greenmount West.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Up to $17,000 in down payment and closing cost assistance for eligible Johns Hopkins University employees purchasing a home in qualifying Healthy Neighborhoods in Baltimore City. Since 2009, more than $10 million has been provided to over 1,500 employees. Qualifying neighborhoods include Remington, Better Waverly, Waverly, Bayview, Highlandtown, Patterson Park, Ednor Gardens, Charles North, Mount Vernon, and Greenmount West.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Johns Hopkins University employees who want to purchase a home in Baltimore City, particularly in select qualifying Healthy Neighborhoods near the Hopkins campus.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Down payment and closing cost assistance for a home purchase in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Homes must be located in qualifying Healthy Neighborhoods in Baltimore City: Remington, Better Waverly, Waverly, Bayview, Highlandtown, Patterson Park, Ednor Gardens, Charles North, Mount Vernon, and Greenmount West.
requirements_list: Must be a Johns Hopkins University employee
Must purchase a home in one of the qualifying Healthy Neighborhoods in Baltimore City
May require certified homeownership counseling
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact Healthy Neighborhoods, Inc. or Johns Hopkins University HR for application details. More information is available at https://hr.jhu.edu/benefits-worklife/live-near-your-work/ and https://www.healthyneighborhoods.org/buyer-incentive-resources.

structured_extraction.program_description: BUILD College is a program run by Johns Hopkins University that provides training and development for design and construction firms. It is currently accepting applications for its 11th cohort.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Structured training program for design and construction firms. Currently accepting applications for the 11th cohort.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Design and construction firms in Baltimore City
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City area
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply via the BUILD College page on the HopkinsLocal website.

structured_extraction.program_description: An annual program launched in 2012 that supports a cohort of social entrepreneurs from the greater Baltimore area as they build innovative, sustainable, and scalable solutions to social problems. The program is open to any applicant from the greater Baltimore area, not just Johns Hopkins affiliates.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Participants receive support to develop their social ventures. Past awards include a $25,000 prize. The program provides structured support to help social entrepreneurs grow their initiatives.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Social entrepreneurs from the greater Baltimore area seeking to build innovative solutions to social and community challenges.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Building and scaling social ventures that address social, community, health, or economic challenges.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Open to applicants from the greater Baltimore area.
requirements_list: Must be based in the greater Baltimore area
Not restricted to Johns Hopkins affiliates
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply through the Social Innovation Lab website at pavacenter.jhu.edu/social-innovation-lab/.

structured_extraction.program_name: Keeping it SAFE Student Video Contest
structured_extraction.program_description: A video contest run by the Keeping it SAFE: Under Twenty-One Alcohol Prevention Coalition (Montgomery County Alcohol Beverage Services) that invites student teams from Montgomery County public and private high schools and middle schools to create a 30-second public service announcement video about the risks and dangers of underage alcohol use. Winning teams receive cash prizes awarded to their affiliated school or organization, with separate prize tiers for high school and middle school entries, plus an additional prize for the video receiving the most online 'likes.' Participating students in qualifying submissions also receive 5 SSL hours.
structured_extraction.agency: Keeping it SAFE: Under Twenty-One Alcohol Prevention Coalition (Montgomery County Alcohol Beverage Services)
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Cash prizes awarded to schools or organizations on behalf of winning student teams (checks payable to schools or organizations only). High school prizes: 1st place $1,000; 2nd place $500; 3rd place $350; Honorable Mention $100. Middle school prizes: 1st place $500; 2nd place $300; 3rd place $250; Honorable Mention $100. An additional $150 prize is awarded to the video that receives the most 'likes.' Participating students in qualifying submissions receive 5 SSL hours each.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Student teams of two or more students (grades 6–12) enrolled in Montgomery County public or private schools or in faith-based or service-based organizations
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Cash prizes are awarded to the affiliated school or organization (checks payable to schools or organizations only); participating students in qualifying submissions receive 5 SSL hours
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Open to students enrolled in Montgomery County public or private schools or in faith-based or service-based organizations in Montgomery County, MD
requirements_list: Teams must consist of two or more students
Students must be enrolled in a Montgomery County public or private school, or a faith-based or service-based organization
Video entry must be exactly 30 seconds in length (entries over 30 seconds will be disqualified)
Video must address one of the three specified topics about underage alcohol use risks
No copyrighted materials may be used without permission
No glorification of substance use or violence; no branded products
Video must be 16:9 aspect ratio, 720p resolution or higher
Each participating student must submit a consent and release form
Entries must be submitted via online application with a link to the video
All entries become KIS Coalition property for public information use
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Fill out the online application form and submit a public shared file link (e.g. Dropbox, Google Drive) to your video entry, including a slate/credits. Each participating student must also complete a separate consent and release form. Entries were due March 23, 2025 by 4:00 PM.

structured_extraction.program_description: A Kent County property tax credit for commercial or industrial real property owners who make a capital investment on their property where a business locates to conduct business. The credit is applied against the increased assessed value of the property for ten years: 50% for years 1–5, 25% for years 6–7, and 15% for years 8–10.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Property tax credit against the increased assessed value of the property for 10 years: 50% credit for years 1-5; 25% credit for years 6-7; 15% credit for years 8-10.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Commercial or industrial real property owners in Kent County making capital investments where a business entity locates to conduct business
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Reduction in property tax on the increased assessed value resulting from capital investment
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Kent County, Maryland
requirements_list: Must own commercial or industrial real property in Kent County
Must make a capital investment on the property
A business entity must locate on the property to conduct business
Adopted June 6, 2017; effective July 20, 2017
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Download and complete the Application for Commerce Zone Tax Credit from the program website and submit to Kent County.

structured_extraction.program_name: Kent County Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund (CRRF) Small Grant Program
structured_extraction.program_description: The Kent County CRRF Small Grant Program awards small grants up to $4,000 on a rolling basis to support initiatives that benefit low-income communities in Kent County. The county makes approximately $20,000 available annually, distributed through quarterly funding decisions throughout the year. Applications are reviewed and funding decisions are made four times per year (February, May, August, and November) until annual allocations are expended.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants of up to $4,000 per request. Approximately $20,000 is available annually, distributed quarterly until funds are exhausted. Applications are reviewed quarterly with funding decisions made by award dates: February 15, May 15, August 15, and November 15.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Rolling basis, reviewed quarterly: Oct 1–Dec 31 (award by Feb 15), Jan 1–Mar 31 (award by May 15), Apr 1–Jun 30 (award by Aug 15), Jul 1–Sep 30 (award by Nov 15)
structured_extraction.program_audience: Local nonprofits, community groups, individuals, and other organizations serving low-income communities in Kent County
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Allowable initiatives that benefit low-income communities in Kent County, as defined in program guidelines.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Kent County, Maryland
requirements_list: Project must benefit low-income communities in Kent County
Requests must support allowable initiatives as defined in program guidelines
Maximum request is $4,000
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Submit an application during one of the quarterly submission windows (October–December, January–March, April–June, or July–September). Applications are reviewed quarterly and funding decisions are made within approximately six weeks after each submission period closes (by February 15, May 15, August 15, and November 15 respectively), until annual allocations are expended. Contact Joanne McNamara at jmcnamara@kentgov.org with questions.

structured_extraction.program_name: Kent County Opioid Restitution Fund (ORF) Small Grant Program
structured_extraction.program_description: The Kent County ORF Small Grant Program awards small grants of up to $4,000 on a rolling basis to fund opioid abatement activities that meet the requirements of the National Settlement Agreements. The county makes approximately $20,000 available annually, distributed through quarterly funding decisions throughout the year. Applications are reviewed four times per year (February, May, August, and November award cycles) until annual allocations are expended.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants of up to $4,000 per request. A total of approximately $20,000 is available annually, distributed quarterly until funds are exhausted. Funded from opioid national settlement agreement proceeds. Applications are reviewed quarterly with funding decisions made by February 15, May 15, August 15, and November 15 corresponding to four submission windows (Oct 1–Dec 31, Jan 1–Mar 31, Apr 1–Jun 30, Jul 1–Sep 30).
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Rolling basis, reviewed quarterly: Oct 1–Dec 31 (award by Feb 15), Jan 1–Mar 31 (award by May 15), Apr 1–Jun 30 (award by Aug 15), Jul 1–Sep 30 (award by Nov 15); reviewed through September 30, 2026
structured_extraction.program_audience: Local nonprofits, community groups, individuals, and other organizations in Kent County seeking funding for opioid abatement activities.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Allowable opioid abatement activities as defined under the terms of the National Settlement Agreements (see Exhibit E).
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Kent County, Maryland
requirements_list: Funded activities must qualify as allowable opioid abatement activities under the National Settlement Agreements (see Exhibit E)
Maximum request is $4,000
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Submit an application and budget using the provided forms during one of the quarterly submission windows (October–December, January–March, April–June, or July–September). Funding decisions are made within approximately six weeks after each submission period closes (by February 15, May 15, August 15, and November 15), until annual allocations are expended. Contact Joanne McNamara at jmcnamara@kentgov.org with questions.

structured_extraction.program_name: Tax Credits for Businesses That Create New Jobs (County)
structured_extraction.program_description: A Kent County property tax credit for businesses that construct or expand their premises and create new full-time jobs. To qualify, a business must build or expand its facility by at least 5,000 square feet and hire at least 10 new full-time employees. The credit is applied against the increased assessed value of the property for six years.
